scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: Ten independent interpretation, argument and critical-transfer questions, pending teacher review.

questions.q: Why does the author reject the label 'bad writing' for informal messages?
choices: The style is often a deliberate register suited to a relationship.
Instant messages are always written with complete accuracy.
Spelling conventions no longer exist for digital communication.
Messages can never be preserved or quoted after sending.
questions.explanation: The essay treats informal spelling as social choice, not automatically lack of competence.

questions.q: What is the wider purpose of describing messaging conventions as a 'repair kit'?
choices: They guarantee identical interpretations across generations.
They compensate partly for nonverbal cues absent from written interaction.
They convert every informal message into a legal document.
They prevent other users from sharing screenshots.
questions.explanation: Emojis, repeated letters and lowercase can restore aspects of spoken tone and rhythm.

questions.q: What is lost when a screenshot becomes evidence outside its original audience?
choices: The exact letters that were originally typed.
The ability to reproduce the message's visual appearance.
The shared history and conversational situation that shaped the words.
The possibility that a screenshot will be forwarded.
questions.explanation: Context collapse preserves a phrase while stripping out the surrounding exchange.

questions.q: Why does the writer pose a question about several parties' responsibility?
choices: To prove that the screenshot editor is always innocent.
To claim that the original writer can never make a mistake.
To identify the precise school sanction that should follow.
To show that blame cannot be assigned adequately to only one actor.
questions.explanation: The hypothetical case exposes responsibility across composing, cropping and sharing.

questions.q: What paradox lies in treating messages as speech when writing but documents when reading?
choices: We believe informal messages disappear faster than spoken remarks.
We expect conversational freedom as senders but documentary certainty as readers.
We demand that every typed exchange follow a legal format.
We never consider whether an audience has changed.
questions.explanation: The essay identifies conflicting assumptions about the same medium.

questions.q: Why does the author note that deleting a message cannot remove existing copies?
choices: To argue that applications should prevent every screenshot.
To show that all messages have already become public.
To imply that deletion has no legitimate purpose.
To limit expectations of what a technical fix can accomplish.
questions.explanation: The technological limitation supports the need for a broader ethic of interpretation.

questions.q: A parent receives a screenshot without the emojis that framed a joke. What would responsible interpretation involve?
choices: Requesting the preceding conversation before deciding the writer's intent.
Judging the excerpt solely from its most literal reading.
Forwarding the cropped image to more parents.
Assuming every joke must be harmless regardless of content.
questions.explanation: The example shows that omitted signals can drastically alter perceived meaning.

questions.q: A new student misreads the group's ironic use of punctuation. What may explain the misunderstanding?
choices: The group has stopped using language altogether.
Every member consciously means to insult newcomers.
The student does not yet share the group's communicative code.
Punctuation carries no social meaning in any context.
questions.explanation: Messaging cues work quickly among people who share conventions, not always for newcomers.

questions.q: A teacher asks pupils to investigate a screenshot before condemning its author. Which skill is being practised?
choices: Learning to delete all embarrassing messages from phones.
Reconstructing audience and context instead of relying on an isolated quotation.
Ensuring that every student uses the same emoji.
Writing faster messages during group projects.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph describes a literacy exercise that replaces outrage with inquiry.

questions.q: Which combination best reflects the author's proposed ethical approach?
choices: Writers avoid all jokes; readers treat every screenshot as conclusive.
Writers publish only formal texts; readers ignore possible harm.
Writers rely on delete functions; readers never ask further questions.
Writers consider future circulation; readers allow room for missing context.
questions.explanation: The essay asks both parties to respond to the medium's durability and ambiguity.
